meta.title: Inside Combustion — how engines really work
meta.description: An interactive, 3D guide to internal combustion engines: four-stroke, diesel, two-stroke and Wankel, with live physics, tools and games. Clear enough for a 10-year-old, deep enough for an engineer.
meta.ogAlt: A cutaway of a single-cylinder engine with glowing combustion in the cylinder

block.name: Cylinder block
block.role: The heavy metal body that holds the cylinder, where the piston slides up and down.

head.name: Cylinder head
head.role: The lid on top of the cylinder. It holds the valves, ports and spark plug.

crankcase.name: Crankcase
crankcase.role: The case around the crankshaft. It keeps the oil in and holds the bearings.

oilpan.name: Oil pan
oilpan.role: A tray under the engine that holds the oil.

camcover.name: Cam cover
camcover.role: A lid that keeps oil around the camshafts and dirt out.

crankshaft.name: Crankshaft
crankshaft.role: Turns the up-and-down push of the piston into spinning, like the pedals on a bike.

rod.name: Connecting rod
rod.role: Links the piston to the crankshaft and carries the push between them.

piston.name: Piston
piston.role: A sliding metal plug. Burning gas pushes it down; it squeezes gas on the way up.

intakeValve.name: Intake valve
intakeValve.role: A door that opens to let fresh air and fuel into the cylinder.

exhaustValve.name: Exhaust valve
exhaustValve.role: A door that opens to let burned gas out of the cylinder.

intakeCam.name: Intake camshaft
intakeCam.role: A spinning shaft with a bump that pushes the intake valve open at the right moment.

exhaustCam.name: Exhaust camshaft
exhaustCam.role: A spinning shaft with a bump that pushes the exhaust valve open at the right moment.

sparkPlug.name: Spark plug
sparkPlug.role: Makes a tiny electric spark that lights the fuel and air.

coil.name: Ignition coil
coil.role: Turns the car’s low battery voltage into the very high voltage the spark needs.

injector.name: Diesel injector
injector.role: Sprays diesel fuel at very high pressure straight into the hot air.

glowPlug.name: Glow plug
glowPlug.role: A small heater that helps a cold diesel engine start.

intake.name: Intake manifold
intake.role: Pipes that guide fresh air to the cylinder.

exhaust.name: Exhaust manifold
exhaust.role: A pipe that carries hot burned gas away. It glows when the engine works hard.

timingBelt.name: Timing belt
timingBelt.role: Links the crankshaft to the camshafts so the valves move in step with the piston.

throttle.name: Throttle
throttle.role: A flap that controls how much air gets in — that is what the accelerator pedal moves.

catalyst.name: Catalytic converter
catalyst.role: Cleans the exhaust by turning harmful gases into less harmful ones.

portInjector.name: Fuel injector
portInjector.role: Sprays a fine mist of petrol into the incoming air.

rotor.name: Rotor
rotor.role: A rounded triangle that spins inside the housing and does the job of the pistons.

housing.name: Rotor housing
housing.role: The oval-ish chamber the rotor spins in.

eshaft.name: Eccentric shaft
eshaft.role: The output shaft. It turns three times for every turn of the rotor.

transfer.name: Transfer port
transfer.role: A channel that moves fresh mixture from the crankcase up into the cylinder.

exPort.name: Exhaust port
exPort.role: A hole in the cylinder wall. When the piston uncovers it, burned gas rushes out.

inPort.name: Intake port
inPort.role: Lets fresh mixture into the crankcase while the piston rises.

hero.title: Inside Combustion
hero.sub: Thousands of tiny explosions a minute, tamed into smooth spinning power. Take the engine apart, slow time down and see exactly how it works.
hero.stageLabel: A single-cylinder petrol engine turning slowly. A warm glow appears in the cylinder each time the fuel burns.

big-idea.title: The big idea
big-idea.takeaway: An engine turns fuel into motion by burning it in a closed space, again and again.
big-idea.lede: Every car engine on this page follows the same simple recipe. Learn it once and the rest will make sense.
big-idea.see: A single-cylinder engine seen from the side. The camera follows the gas: in through the intake, squeezed by the piston, lit by the spark, pushing the piston down and spinning the crankshaft.

beats.t: Fuel needs oxygen to burn, just like a campfire. The engine pulls in air and mixes it with a little fuel.
A [[piston]] squeezes the mixture into a tiny space. Squeezed gas gets hot and burns much better.
A spark lights the mixture. The hot gas expands fast and pushes the piston down hard.
The [[crankshaft]] turns that push into spinning, like your legs turning bicycle pedals. The spin drives the wheels.

big-idea.why: Burning fuel releases a lot of energy from a small amount of liquid. That is why engines can move heavy cars for hundreds of kilometres on one tank.
big-idea.safety: Fuel and engines are dangerous: they get very hot, the parts move with great force and fuel catches fire easily. Please explore them here, not at home.
deeper: An [[internal-combustion|internal combustion engine]] is a heat engine: it turns heat into mechanical work. The fuel burns inside the engine, so the hot gas itself does the pushing.
No heat engine can turn all of its heat into work. Physics sets a ceiling, and real engines lose more heat to cooling, exhaust and friction. You will see where it all goes in the efficiency section.

anatomy.title: Engine anatomy
anatomy.takeaway: About a dozen key parts work together, and each one has a single clear job.
anatomy.lede: Watch a single-cylinder engine build itself, part by part. Hover or tap any part to see what it does.
anatomy.see: The engine assembles in order: block, crankshaft, piston and connecting rod, cylinder head, camshafts, valves, spark plug, then the intake and exhaust.
anatomy.try: Press “Build it”, then step through the parts. Switch to “Find the part” and test yourself.
anatomy.why: Knowing the parts lets you follow how the gas moves and where the push goes, step by step.

steps.t: The **cylinder block** is the engine’s strong body. Inside it is the round **cylinder**.
The **crankshaft** sits at the bottom. It has an offset part, called a crank, just like a bike pedal.
The **piston** slides in the cylinder. Rings around it seal the gap so gas cannot leak past.
The **connecting rod** links piston and crankshaft. It swings a little as the crank turns.
The **cylinder head** closes the top. Channels in it, called ports, lead gas in and out.
Two **camshafts** spin on top. A timing belt turns them at exactly half the crankshaft’s speed.
The **valves** are little doors. A bump on each camshaft pushes its valve open, and a spring closes it.
The **spark plug** sits in the middle of the head, right above the burning space.
Finally the **intake** brings air in and the **exhaust** carries burned gas away.

deeper: The cylinder head of this model has two overhead camshafts, one for the intake valve and one for the exhaust valve. Many real engines have four valves per cylinder: two intake and two exhaust, for better breathing.
The block in the cutaway view shows a hollow ring around the cylinder. That is the **water jacket**: coolant flows through it and carries heat away to the radiator.
The crankshaft has heavy **counterweights** opposite the crankpin. They balance the spinning mass so the engine shakes less.

four-stroke.title: Four-stroke petrol engine
four-stroke.takeaway: Four strokes — suck, squeeze, bang, blow — and the crankshaft turns twice.
four-stroke.lede: This is the engine in most petrol cars, invented by Nikolaus Otto’s company in 1876. Scroll to move the piston through the cycle yourself.
four-stroke.see: A cutaway single-cylinder petrol engine. Cyan particles are fresh air and fuel, they warm up as they are squeezed, glow white-hot when the spark lights them, and turn grey as they leave through the exhaust.
four-stroke.try: Drag the speed slider to redline and watch the flame. Then switch to Cutaway or X-ray and slow it down to 0.05×.
four-stroke.why: Doing the four jobs in separate strokes keeps fresh charge and burned gas apart. That makes the engine clean and efficient for its size.

strokes.t: The piston slides down and the intake [[valve]] is open. Air and a fine mist of fuel rush in — like air filling a syringe when you pull the plunger.
Both valves close. The piston moves up and squeezes the mixture into a space about ten times smaller. Squeezed gas gets hot, like a bicycle pump that warms up when you pump fast.
Just before the top, the [[spark-plug|spark plug]] fires. The mixture burns in a split second. The hot gas presses on the piston and shoves it down. Only this stroke makes power.
The exhaust valve opens. The piston rises and pushes the burned gas out. Then the intake valve opens and it all starts again.

four-stroke.pvCaption: This chart shows the pressure inside the cylinder (up) against the space the gas has (sideways). The dot follows the 3D engine. The shaded loop is the work done in one cycle.
deeper: **Crank angle.** One full cycle takes 720° of crank rotation: intake 0–180°, compression 180–360°, power 360–540°, exhaust 540–720°. The model computes the piston position from the crank geometry: x(θ) = r·cos θ + √(l² − r²·sin² θ), with r = half the [[stroke]] and l = the rod length.

**Valve timing {typ}.** Valves do not open exactly at the dead centres. The intake opens about 10° before [[tdc|top dead centre]] and closes about 45° after bottom dead centre, so the moving air keeps filling the cylinder. The exhaust opens about 45° before bottom dead centre. Near the top, both are briefly open: this is [[valve-overlap|overlap]].
**Spark timing.** The flame needs time to spread, so the spark comes 10–30° before the top. The faster the engine turns, the earlier the spark.

**Pressure model.** Compression and expansion follow p·Vⁿ = constant with n ≈ 1.3. Burning is modelled with a Wiebe function, x_b(θ) = 1 − exp(−a·((θ − θ₀)/Δθ)^(m+1)), with a ≈ 5 and m ≈ 2. Peak pressure here is about 50–65 bar at full throttle.
**Compression ratio {typ}.** Petrol engines use about 9–14:1. Higher would be more efficient, but the mixture would start to [[knock]].

figures.l: of crank rotation in one cycle
peak pressure at full throttle in this model

diesel.title: Diesel engine
diesel.takeaway: A diesel has no spark plug: it squeezes air so hard that the air itself lights the fuel.
diesel.lede: Rudolf Diesel patented the idea in 1892 and ran his first working engine in 1897. Today diesels move most trucks, trains and ships.
diesel.see: A cutaway diesel engine. Only air comes in. Near the top, the injector sprays five thin plumes of fuel into the very hot air, and the flame starts at their tips.
diesel.try: Slide “Fuel” up and down. A diesel has no throttle flap: it makes more power simply by injecting more fuel.
diesel.why: Higher squeeze means more of the fuel’s energy becomes motion. Diesels are the most efficient engines on the road.

cards.t: A diesel squeezes air about 15 to 20 times {typ}. The air gets hot enough — several hundred degrees Celsius — to light diesel fuel by itself.
An [[fuel-injector|injector]] sprays fuel at very high pressure, just before the top. The fuel lights within a few thousandths of a second.
On a cold morning the air may not get hot enough. A [[glow-plug|glow plug]] warms the chamber to help the engine start.
High pressure needs a thick, strong engine. Diesels are heavier and noisier, but they pull hard at low speed — they make a lot of [[torque]].

diesel.dirtyTitle: Why diesels used to be dirty
diesel.dirty: Burning fuel droplets can leave tiny soot particles, and very hot burning makes nitrogen oxides ([[nox|NOx]]). Modern diesels catch soot in a [[particulate-filter|particulate filter]] and remove NOx with [[scr|SCR]]: a liquid called AdBlue is sprayed into the exhaust and turns NOx into nitrogen and water.
deeper: **Compression ratio {typ}:** about 14–22:1 for diesels against 9–14:1 for petrol engines. Petrol cannot go that high because it would self-ignite too early and knock. Diesel is meant to self-ignite.

**Combustion.** After injection starts there is a short ignition delay. The fuel that mixed during the delay burns all at once (the sharp first peak), then the rest burns as fast as it can mix with air. The model uses a double Wiebe function for this.

**Load control.** A petrol engine controls power by throttling the air. A diesel lets the air in freely and changes the amount of fuel. That avoids pumping losses at part load, one reason for its high efficiency.
**Efficiency {typ}:** a modern car diesel reaches about 40–45 % at its best point, against roughly 35–41 % for a modern petrol engine.

figures.l: best efficiency of a car diesel {typ}

two-stroke.title: Two-stroke engine
two-stroke.takeaway: A two-stroke does the whole job in one up and one down — a power stroke every turn.
two-stroke.lede: No valves, no camshafts: the piston itself opens and closes holes in the cylinder wall.
two-stroke.see: A cutaway two-stroke engine. As the piston rises, fresh mixture is drawn into the crankcase below it. As it falls, it uncovers the exhaust port first, then the transfer ports that push fresh mixture up into the cylinder.
two-stroke.try: Slow it to 0.05× and watch the exhaust port open just before the transfer ports.
two-stroke.why: Twice as many power strokes from the same size makes small two-strokes light and punchy — great for chainsaws, mopeds and outboard motors.

cards.t: Above the piston, the mixture is squeezed. Below it, the rising piston pulls fresh mixture into the [[crankcase]].
The spark pushes the piston down. It first uncovers the [[ports|exhaust port]], so burned gas escapes. Then the transfer ports open and fresh mixture flows in.
Few moving parts and a power stroke every turn. That is why two-strokes suit tools you carry.
Some fresh fuel escapes straight out of the exhaust. Oil is mixed into the fuel to lubricate the engine, and it burns too, so the exhaust is smoky.

two-stroke.marine: The biggest engines in the world are also two-strokes: the slow diesels that drive container ships. They are very different inside. Air is blown in through ports at the bottom and leaves through a valve at the top ([[uniflow|uniflow scavenging]]). Long [[crosshead|crossheads]] keep side forces off the pistons. Their efficiency is above 50 % {typ}.
deeper: **Port timing {typ}** in this model: exhaust opens about 105° after top dead centre, transfer ports about 120°. Both close again on the way up, symmetrically around bottom dead centre.
**Why exhaust first?** The cylinder pressure must drop below crankcase pressure before the transfer ports open. Otherwise burned gas would rush backwards into the crankcase.

**Scavenging** means pushing burned gas out with fresh charge. In small engines the crankcase acts as a pump. Some fresh charge short-circuits straight to the exhaust: the main reason for high fuel use and hydrocarbon emissions.

wankel.title: Wankel rotary engine
wankel.takeaway: A rounded triangle spins inside an oval and does all four strokes without any back-and-forth parts.
wankel.lede: Felix Wankel’s engine first ran in 1957. Its most famous home is the Mazda RX-7 and RX-8 sports cars.
wankel.see: The rotor orbits inside the housing. Its three faces form three separate chambers. Each one is coloured by its stroke: cyan intake, violet compression, amber power, grey exhaust.
wankel.try: Watch the counters: the output shaft turns three times for each turn of the rotor.
wankel.why: Smooth spinning and very few parts make a rotary engine small and light for its power.

cards.t: While one face sucks in, another squeezes and the third burns. You get one power pulse for every turn of the output shaft.
There are no pistons stopping and starting. The rotor just goes round, so the engine runs very smoothly and revs high.
The tips of the rotor need seals that wear. The long, thin chamber burns fuel less completely, so rotaries use more fuel and oil.

deeper: **Geometry.** The housing is an [[epitrochoid]]: x = e·cos 3α + R·cos α, y = e·sin 3α + R·sin α, where e is the eccentricity and R the rotor radius. The rotor’s flanks are the inner envelope of that curve, so its three tips always touch the housing.
**3:1.** The rotor centre orbits on an eccentric of the output shaft. Gears inside fix the ratio: the shaft turns three times per rotor turn, and each face fires once per rotor turn.
**Displacement** of a rotary is usually given per face, which makes comparisons with piston engines tricky.

layouts.title: Cylinder layouts
layouts.takeaway: Bigger engines use several cylinders, and how you line them up changes how smooth they feel.
layouts.lede: Car engines often have 4, 6 or 8 cylinders. Their pistons take turns firing, so the push on the crankshaft is smoother.
layouts.see: Pistons arranged on one crankshaft. Each cylinder flashes amber when it fires, in the firing order. The meter shows how much the engine wants to shake.
layouts.try: Switch between the layouts and compare the shake meter. Inline-6 and cross-plane V8 stay calm.
layouts.why: Smoothness, size and cost pull in different directions. Car makers choose the layout that fits the car.

i4.name: Inline-4
i4.t: Four cylinders in a row. Compact and cheap — the most common car engine. It has a vibration at twice the engine speed.

i6.name: Inline-6
i6.t: Six in a row. Its forces cancel out naturally, so it runs silky smooth, but it is long.

v8cross.name: Cross-plane V8
v8cross.t: Two banks of four at 90°. Very smooth, with the classic burbling sound.

v8flat.name: Flat-plane V8
v8flat.t: A lighter crankshaft that revs quickly, used in racing engines. It shakes sideways a little.

boxer4.name: Boxer-4
boxer4.t: Two pairs of opposed pistons that punch out and back like boxers. Low and wide.

layouts.orderNote: Firing orders shown are common examples; cylinder numbering differs between makers.
deeper: **Firing orders {ex}:** inline-4 1-3-4-2; inline-6 1-5-3-6-2-4; cross-plane V8 1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2; flat-plane V8 1-5-3-7-4-8-2-6; flat-4 boxer 1-3-2-4. A four-stroke with n cylinders fires every 720°/n of crank rotation.

**Balance.** A piston speeds up and slows down twice per turn. The main shaking force (1st order) can be cancelled by layout or counterweights. A smaller 2nd-order force comes from the rod’s angle and repeats twice per turn. Inline-4: 2nd-order forces add up. Inline-6: all cancel. Cross-plane V8: no 2nd-order forces. Flat-plane V8: a sideways 2nd-order force. Boxer-4: forces cancel, leaving a small rocking couple.
The meter in the model sums these forces in the front view using cos φ and λ·cos 2φ per cylinder, with λ = r/l ≈ 0.29.

systems.title: Engine systems
systems.takeaway: The engine needs helpers: fuel, a spark, oil, cooling and clean-up.
systems.lede: Pick a system to see how it works. The parts it uses light up on the engine.
systems.see: The petrol engine with the parts of the selected system highlighted in amber.
systems.try: Tap each system, then rotate the engine to find the glowing parts.
systems.why: If any helper fails, the engine stops — or worse, it damages itself.

fuel.name: Fuel
fuel.t: A pump in the tank sends petrol forward under pressure. The [[fuel-injector|fuel injector]] opens for a few thousandths of a second and sprays a fine mist into the air. A computer decides exactly how long.

ignition.name: Ignition
ignition.t: The battery gives 12 volts. The [[ignition-coil|ignition coil]] boosts that to tens of thousands of volts, enough to jump the gap in the [[spark-plug|spark plug]] and light the mixture.

oil.name: Lubrication
oil.t: An oil pump pulls oil from the oil pan and pushes it to every bearing. A thin film of oil keeps metal from touching metal, a bit like a water slide.

cooling.name: Cooling
cooling.t: A water pump moves coolant through the water jacket around the cylinder. The hot coolant goes to the [[radiator]] to cool. A [[thermostat]] keeps the engine at the right temperature.

exhaust.name: Exhaust
exhaust.t: Hot exhaust passes through the [[catalytic-converter|catalytic converter]]. Inside, precious metals help turn harmful gases into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen.

deeper: **Fuel pressure {typ}:** port injection works at about 3–5 bar; direct petrol injection at 100–350 bar; diesel common-rail at 1,600–2,500 bar.
**Oil film.** In a running bearing, oil is dragged into the narrowing gap and builds up pressure that lifts the shaft off the metal. This is called hydrodynamic lubrication.
**Coolant** runs at about 90 °C {typ}. The thermostat stays shut when the engine is cold, so it warms up quickly, then opens to send coolant to the radiator.

**Three-way catalyst.** It converts carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides at once, but only if the air–fuel ratio is kept very close to chemically correct. An oxygen sensor in the exhaust lets the engine computer hold it there.

boost.title: Turbochargers and superchargers
boost.takeaway: Squeeze more air in and you can burn more fuel — that means more power from the same engine.
boost.lede: A turbocharger uses the exhaust to spin a fan. A supercharger is driven by the engine itself.
boost.see: Air flows in cyan, exhaust in grey. The turbo’s turbine is spun by exhaust; on the same shaft, its compressor pushes air into the engine.
boost.try: Move the boost slider and watch the torque curve rise. Then press “Accelerate” to see turbo lag.
boost.why: Boost lets a small engine do the work of a big one, so cars can be lighter and use less fuel when cruising.

cards.t: Exhaust gas spins a turbine wheel. A compressor wheel on the same shaft pushes extra air into the engine. It uses energy that would otherwise be wasted.
A belt from the crankshaft drives the compressor. Boost is instant, but it takes some of the engine’s own power.
Squeezing air heats it, and hot air is thin. An [[intercooler]] cools the air so more of it fits in the cylinder.
Too much boost would hurt the engine. A [[wastegate]] lets some exhaust bypass the turbine to hold the boost steady.

boost.lag: Press the pedal and the turbo first has to speed up. For a moment the engine feels like it has no boost. That delay is [[turbo-lag|turbo lag]].
deeper: **Boost** is extra pressure above the atmosphere, usually 0.5–1.5 bar {typ} in road cars. At 1 bar boost the air is about twice as dense — less after heating, which is why intercoolers matter.
**Torque scales with air.** With fuel matched to air, the torque roughly follows the mass of air trapped each cycle. The curve here scales the natural torque with charge density after intercooling.
**Knock limit.** Boosted petrol engines lower the compression ratio or retard the spark to avoid knock.

gearbox.title: From engine to wheels
gearbox.takeaway: An engine only works well within a narrow range of speeds, so a gearbox matches it to the wheels.
gearbox.lede: A car crawls at walking pace and cruises on the motorway. The engine cannot spin from zero to 50,000 rpm, so gears do the translating.
gearbox.see: A simple gearbox demo: the engine speed needle, the selected gear and the road speed. Lines on the chart show each gear.
gearbox.try: Pick 1st gear and press “Accelerate”. Change up near the amber zone and watch the engine speed drop.
gearbox.why: Low gears give a strong push for starting and climbing. High gears let the engine turn slowly and save fuel at speed.

cards.t: A low gear is like a small front sprocket on a bike: easy to push, but you go slowly. High gears are the opposite.
The [[clutch]] connects and disconnects the engine from the gearbox. It lets the engine keep running while the car stands still, and lets you change gear smoothly.
Gears trade speed for force. In 1st gear the wheels get several times more [[torque]] than the engine makes.

deeper: **Road speed** v = (engine rpm / (gear ratio × final drive)) × wheel circumference × 60 / 1000 km/h.
**Ratios {typ}** in this demo: 1st 3.6, 2nd 2.1, 3rd 1.4, 4th 1.0, 5th 0.8, 6th 0.65 with a 3.9 final drive and 2.0 m wheel circumference.
Automatic gearboxes and CVTs do the same job, choosing the ratio for you.

efficiency.title: Efficiency and hybrids
efficiency.takeaway: Most of the fuel’s energy leaves as heat; good engines turn about a third into motion, the best diesels even more.
efficiency.lede: Follow the energy from the tank. The width of each band shows its share at a good operating point {typ}.
efficiency.see: An energy flow diagram. Fuel enters on the left and splits into useful work, heat carried by the coolant, heat in the exhaust, and friction.
efficiency.try: Switch between petrol and diesel and compare how wide the useful-work band is.
efficiency.why: Every bit of saved heat means less fuel burned and less carbon dioxide made.

sankey.note: Typical shares at a good operating point. In everyday driving the useful share is lower.

cards.t: Keep the intake valve open a bit longer, and some mixture is pushed back out. The squeeze becomes shorter than the push, so more energy is captured — at the cost of some power.
A [[hybrid]] adds an electric motor and a battery. The motor helps when pulling away, and braking charges the battery instead of making heat.

hybrid.title: How a hybrid shares the work

modes.stopped: Standing still: the engine can switch off completely.
modes.accelerate: Pulling away: the motor and the engine push together.
modes.cruise: Cruising: the engine runs in its efficient zone and may top up the battery.
modes.brake: Braking: the motor works as a generator and charges the battery.

deeper: **Ideal limits.** Otto cycle: η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1). With r = 10 and γ = 1.4 that is 60 %. Real engines reach about 35–41 % {typ} for petrol because of heat loss, friction, pumping and incomplete burning.
**Atkinson/Miller.** A late-closing intake valve gives an effective compression ratio smaller than the expansion ratio. The ideal Atkinson cycle beats the Otto cycle at the same compression ratio.
**Largest engines.** Big two-stroke marine diesels exceed 50 % {typ}, helped by slow speed, huge size and turbocharging.

history.title: History
history.takeaway: In about forty years, engines went from a curiosity to the heart of the motor car.

items.t: Étienne Lenoir builds one of the first practical internal combustion engines. It burns coal gas without compressing it first, so it is weak and thirsty.
Nikolaus Otto’s company builds a four-stroke engine that compresses the charge before lighting it. It works far better, and the cycle still carries his name.
Carl Benz patents a three-wheeled car powered by a single-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine — often called the first true automobile.
Rudolf Diesel patents an engine that lights fuel with the heat of compressed air (1892). His first working engine runs in 1897.
Felix Wankel’s first running rotary engine replaces pistons with a spinning rotor.

future.title: The future
future.takeaway: Combustion engines are still everywhere, but electric drives are taking a growing share — what happens next is still being decided.
future.lede: Here are the main directions people are working on today. None of them is a sure thing.

cards.t: Better burning, less friction and smarter control keep raising efficiency. Pairing engines with electric motors in hybrids saves the most.
Fuels can be made from hydrogen and carbon dioxide captured from the air, using renewable electricity. Today they are expensive and made only in small amounts.
An engine can burn hydrogen instead of petrol. It makes no carbon dioxide at the tailpipe, but very hot burning still creates nitrogen oxides that must be cleaned.
Battery-electric cars have no combustion at all. They are growing fast in many countries, while ships, planes and heavy machines will likely rely on combustion for longer.

lab.title: Tools lab
lab.takeaway: Change the numbers and see what an engineer sees.
lab.lede: Every tool here uses the same physics as the 3D models. The P–V chart and valve wheel follow the four-stroke engine above.

pv.t: The engine’s heartbeat chart. Pressure goes up, volume goes sideways. The area inside the loop is the work of one cycle.

valve.t: One full cycle is 720°. The arcs show when each valve is open. Drag them to shift the camshafts and watch the loop change.

disp.t: How much air all the pistons sweep in one turn of the cycle.

cr.t: How much the engine squeezes, and the ideal efficiency that brings.

curve.t: Build an engine and read its torque and power at any speed.

lab.crNote: Petrol engines usually stay below about 14:1 {typ}: above that the mixture tends to knock — it explodes on its own instead of burning smoothly.
lab.powerNote: Power is calculated from torque: P [kW] = T [N·m] × rpm / 9549.

compare.takeaway: Put any two engines side by side and run them in sync.
compare.lede: Pick two engines. They share one clock, so you can compare how often each one makes power.

glossary.def: A machine that turns energy into motion.
An engine that burns its fuel inside itself, so the hot gas pushes the parts directly.
The round tube inside the engine where the piston slides up and down.
A metal plug that slides in the cylinder. Gas pushes it, or it squeezes gas.
The shaft that turns the pistons’ up-and-down motion into spinning, like bicycle pedals.
The bar that links the piston to the crankshaft.
A spinning shaft with egg-shaped bumps (cams) that push the valves open.
A little door in the cylinder head that opens to let gas in or out.
A short moment near the top of the stroke when both the intake and exhaust valves are slightly open.
A part that makes a small electric spark to light the fuel and air.
A part that raises the battery’s voltage high enough to make a spark.
Burning: fuel joins with oxygen and gives off heat.
Squeezing a gas into a smaller space. It raises its pressure and temperature.
How many times smaller the gas space gets when the piston rises. 10:1 means ten times smaller.
One movement of the piston from top to bottom or back. Also the distance it travels.
An engine cycle with four piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust.
An engine cycle that does the whole job in two strokes, so it fires every turn.
The highest point of the piston, where it stops for an instant before coming back down.
The lowest point of the piston.
Revolutions per minute: how many full turns the crankshaft makes in one minute.
Turning force. More torque means a stronger twist on the wheels.
How fast work is done. Power = torque × speed. Measured in kilowatts (kW) or horsepower (hp).
The total space all the pistons sweep through. A bigger number usually means a stronger engine.
The width (diameter) of the cylinder.
An electric nozzle that sprays a precise amount of fuel.
A small electric heater that helps a cold diesel start.
An engine where very hot, squeezed air lights the fuel without a spark.
When part of the mixture explodes on its own before the flame reaches it. It makes a pinging noise and can damage the engine.
A fan driven by exhaust gas that pushes extra air into the engine.
A compressor driven by the engine itself that pushes extra air in.
Extra air pressure made by a turbocharger or supercharger.
A radiator that cools squeezed air before it enters the engine, so more air fits.
A valve that lets some exhaust bypass a turbo’s turbine to limit boost.
The short delay before a turbo spins up and gives full boost.
The share of the fuel’s energy that becomes useful work.
A part in the exhaust that turns harmful gases into less harmful ones.
A filter in a diesel’s exhaust that traps soot.
Selective catalytic reduction: a system that removes nitrogen oxides from diesel exhaust using a liquid called AdBlue.
Nitrogen oxides: polluting gases made when burning is very hot.
Keeping a thin film of oil between moving parts so they do not rub and wear.
A heat exchanger at the front of the car where air cools the hot coolant.
A valve that keeps the coolant shut in until the engine is warm.
A set of gears that matches engine speed to wheel speed.
A coupling that connects or disconnects the engine and gearbox.
The sequence in which the cylinders fire.
The housing around the crankshaft.
Holes or channels that let gas in or out of the cylinder.
Pushing burned gas out of the cylinder with fresh air or mixture.
Gas flows one way through the cylinder: in through ports at the bottom, out through a valve at the top.
An extra sliding joint in very large engines that keeps sideways force off the piston.
A rotary engine where a rounded triangle spins in an oval-ish housing.
The curve traced by a point on a circle rolling around another circle. It shapes a Wankel housing.
A car that combines a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery.
An engine cycle where the expansion is longer than the compression, to capture more energy.
A chart of pressure against volume in the cylinder. The loop area equals the work done.
A unit of pressure. Air around us is about 1 bar.
A unit of power. 1 kW = 1.341 horsepower.
The gases and particles an engine releases.
Fuel made from hydrogen and carbon dioxide using electricity, instead of from crude oil.
How well the forces from moving parts cancel each other out, so the engine does not shake.
A toothed belt that keeps the camshafts turning in step with the crankshaft.
A flap that controls how much air the engine can take in.

quiz.q: In a four-stroke engine, which stroke makes the power?
quiz.why: Only the power stroke is pushed by burning gas. The other three use some of the energy stored in the spinning crankshaft.

quiz.q: How many times does the crankshaft turn in one four-stroke cycle?
quiz.why: Each stroke is half a turn, so four strokes take two full turns (720°).

quiz.q: What lights the fuel in a diesel engine?
quiz.why: A diesel squeezes air so much that it becomes hot enough to light the fuel when it is sprayed in. The glow plug only helps cold starts.

quiz.q: Which part turns the up-and-down motion into spinning?
quiz.why: The crankshaft works like bicycle pedals: pushes on the crank turn the shaft.

quiz.q: How often does a two-stroke engine fire?
quiz.why: A two-stroke completes its cycle in one turn, so it fires every turn.

quiz.q: What spins a turbocharger?
quiz.why: Exhaust gas spins the turbine. A supercharger is the one driven by a belt.

quiz.q: Why does a car need a gearbox?
a: Because the engine works well only in a narrow speed range
quiz.why: Gears let the engine stay in its useful speed range while the car goes from walking pace to motorway speed.

quiz.q: What replaces the pistons in a Wankel engine?
quiz.why: The rotor spins inside the housing and forms three chambers at once.

quiz.q: What does a catalytic converter do?
a: Turns harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones
quiz.why: Inside, precious metals help convert carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides.

quiz.q: Which layout is naturally the smoothest of these?
quiz.why: In an inline-6 the shaking forces of the pistons cancel each other out.

quiz.q: Where does most of the fuel’s energy go in a typical car engine?
a: Out as heat in the exhaust and coolant
quiz.why: Roughly two thirds leaves as heat. Only about a third or less becomes useful work.

quiz.q: Who is the four-stroke cycle named after?
quiz.why: Otto’s company built the successful four-stroke engine in 1876, and it is often called the Otto cycle.

quiz.q: Why does the intake valve close about 45° after bottom dead centre?
a: Because the moving air keeps flowing in after the piston stops
quiz.why: The air column has momentum. Closing late lets it keep filling the cylinder, which improves breathing at speed.

quiz.q: What is the ideal Otto efficiency at a compression ratio of 10 with γ = 1.4?
quiz.why: η = 1 − 1/10^0.4 ≈ 0.60. Real engines get far less because of heat loss, friction and pumping.

quiz.q: How does a diesel control its power?
a: By changing the amount of fuel injected
quiz.why: Diesels run unthrottled and vary fuel quantity, which avoids throttling losses at part load.

quiz.q: In a piston-ported two-stroke, why does the exhaust port open before the transfer ports?
a: So cylinder pressure drops before fresh charge enters
quiz.why: If the transfer ports opened first, high-pressure burned gas would flow back into the crankcase.

quiz.q: How many times does a Wankel’s output shaft turn per rotor revolution?
quiz.why: The rotor centre rides on an eccentric of the shaft, and internal gears fix a 3:1 ratio.

quiz.q: Which statement about balance is correct?
a: A cross-plane V8 has no second-order forces
A flat-plane V8 is smoother than an inline-6
An inline-6 has large second-order forces
quiz.why: The cross-plane crank cancels second-order forces; an inline-4 has a second-order shake at twice engine speed.

quiz.q: An engine makes 300 N·m at 5,000 rpm. Roughly how much power is that?
What does an intercooler do?
a: Cools the exhaust to protect the turbo
Cools the compressed intake air so it is denser
quiz.why: Compression heats the air; cooling it back down packs more air mass into each cylinder.

quiz.q: In an Atkinson-cycle engine…
a: the compression is longer than the expansion
the expansion is longer than the effective compression
the spark comes after top dead centre
quiz.why: Late intake valve closing shortens the effective compression, while the full expansion stroke extracts more work.

quiz.q: What is knock?
a: Mixture self-igniting before the flame arrives
quiz.why: End-gas auto-ignition creates sharp pressure waves. It limits the compression ratio of petrol engines.

quiz.q: Which engines exceed 50 % efficiency?
quiz.why: Huge, slow marine diesels with turbocharging and long expansion are the most efficient combustion engines.

quiz.q: In 1st gear (3.6 × 3.9 final drive), the wheel torque is about how many times the engine torque (ignoring losses)?
quiz.why: Overall ratio = 3.6 × 3.9 ≈ 14, so torque is multiplied by about 14 (and speed divided by 14).
